analysis.one_liner: Toughens coal mine safety rules after disasters: emergency air, communications, tracking, rescue teams, and bigger fines.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote and died when the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After a series of coal mine disasters, this bill would have directed the Labor Department within 90 days to write new rules requiring coal operators to quickly report mine accidents, maintain trained rescue teams on site, stock emergency air supplies and breathing equipment, install two-way communication and electronic tracking for every miner underground, and stop venting mines through belt haulage entries [S2] [S3]. It would also have set minimum penalties of $10,000 for negligent safety violations and up to $100,000 for failing to report an accident, created a research office for mine safety technology, and established a Miner Ombudsman so miners could confidentially report safety problems [S2] [S3]. The Senate referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it [S1] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Underground coal miners and their families, who would get emergency air caches, breathing devices, communications and tracking equipment, guaranteed on-site rescue teams, faster accident reporting, a confidential channel to report safety violations, and stiffer penalties for careless operators [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires every coal mine to stock emergency air supplies, self-contained breathing equipment, and independent two-way communication with the surface at strategic underground locations for miners awaiting rescue [S3].

Requires each miner underground to carry a portable communications device and an electronic tracking device so rescuers can locate them, and requires operators to maintain trained mine rescue teams familiar with their own mine for immediate response [S3].
Sets a $10,000 floor on civil penalties for negligent or reckless safety violations and penalties up to $100,000 for failing to quickly report an accident requiring rescue [S3].

Creates a Miner Ombudsman in the Labor Department's Inspector General office with a toll-free line and website so miners can confidentially report safety violations, and bans venting active working areas through belt haulage entries [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Coal mine operators, who would bear the cost of on-site rescue teams, emergency air and breathing equipment, communications and tracking systems for every miner, and penalties of $10,000 to $100,000 for negligent violations or late accident reporting [S3].

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on mine operators, including small operators, for rescue teams, emergency equipment caches, and a communication and tracking device for every person underground, with no federal funding provided for operators [S3].

The bill works entirely through new Labor Department regulations written within 90 days on topics like rescue team liability and insurance, so the details miners actually get would depend on how those rules are drafted [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For underground miners the benefits are direct and serious: survivable air, a way to call the surface, and a way for rescuers to find them, requirements that follow directly from mine disasters where trapped miners could not be reached [S3]. The costs are real but conventional equipment and training spending borne by operators, and the penalty floor targets operators already showing negligence. The main weakness is that the bill delegates everything to rulemaking on a 90-day clock rather than writing the standards into law itself.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Sen. Robert Byrd of West Virginia introduced the bill on February 1, 2006, joined by original cosponsors Sens. Rockefeller and Kennedy [S1] [S3].
Thirteen senators cosponsored the bill, ten Democrats and three Republicans [S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on February 1, 2006, and no further action was recorded for the rest of the Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal operators were better off, since they avoided the emergency equipment, on-site rescue team, tracking, and penalty requirements for the rest of the Congress; miners got none of these protections from this bill.

for.name: Sen. Robert Byrd
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Sen. Mike Enzi
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup or vote on the bill, which sat in the committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan — 10 Democrats and 3 Republicans cosponsored — but the committee never took it up, so there is no vote record showing how the parties split.

industries.note: Operators would have paid for on-site rescue teams, emergency air and breathing equipment, communication and tracking devices for every miner, and fines of $10,000 to $100,000 for negligent violations or late accident reporting. Their cost is the miners' safety margin.

industries.industry: Mine safety equipment and communications manufacturers
industries.note: The bill would have created demand for breathing equipment, refuge supplies, two-way communication systems, and electronic tracking devices for every person underground, and a new MSHA office to push new safety technologies into mines.
